fields.title: Women Who Moved Heaven
fields.description: Have you ever wondered how women changed the course of history from quiet rooms and tear-stained benches? This book reveals their secret: the power of persistent prayer. From Monica’s seventeen-year intercession to Corrie ten Boom’s faith in a concentration camp, discover how these warriors held heaven open.

fields.title: Introduction: Women Who Held Heaven Open
fields.body_html:
There is a thread running through the whole of church history that is easy to overlook in the official accounts. It does not belong to councils and synods, to theological disputations or institutional records. It belongs to the quiet rooms, the pre-dawn kneelings, the tear-stained prayers breathed over sleeping children, over suffering strangers, over the darkest circumstances the world could devise. It belongs to women. Again and again across twenty centuries, God has answered the prayers of women whose faith was no less formidable for being largely invisible to the crowds, whose intercessions were no less powerful for going largely unrecorded in the history books.

The Scripture is unambiguous on this point. The prophet Joel declared what God Himself had promised for the last days: “Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions. Even on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days” (Joel 2:28–29, NIV). The Spirit of God is no respecter of gender in His distribution of power and calling. The women in this book took that promise at full face value and lived it out with a depth and consistency that shook the world around them.

The first recorded prayer meeting after the ascension of Christ included women at its very core.

Luke describes the gathered disciples: “They all joined together constantly in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers” (Acts 1:14, NIV). And when, in Acts 16, Paul and Silas arrived at Philippi and went looking for a place of prayer on the Sabbath, they found a gathering of women already deep in intercession: “where we expected to find a place of prayer. We sat down and began to speak to the women who had gathered there” (Acts 16:13, NIV). The first European convert was Lydia — a woman found at prayer. From the earliest hours of the church, women have been foundational to its prayer life.

What is a woman who is a prayer warrior? She is not necessarily a woman of public prominence or ecclesiastical authority. She may be, like Monica of Hippo, a mother pressing through seventeen years of unanswered prayer with nothing visible to show for her intercession but a wayward son and an unshakable confidence in the faithfulness of God. She may be, like Corrie ten Boom, a prisoner in a Nazi concentration camp who sustained a prayer meeting in her barracks even as the world around her descended into horror.

She may be, like Lottie Moon, a woman who gave her food away until she was too weak to stand, spending her last earthly breath in prayer for the people she had come to love. She may be known only to God and to the few whose lives she transformed through intercession they never fully knew was happening.

What unites these ten women is precisely the thing that Jesus promised to all who would receive it: access to the Father through the Son that no circumstance, no institution, and no human power could revoke. Jesus declared: “Very truly I tell you, my Father will give you whatever you ask in my name. Until now you have not asked for anything in my name. Ask and you will receive, and your joy will be complete” (John 16:23–24, NIV). These women believed that promise with the whole force of their lives. They did not believe it theoretically. They staked everything on it — their futures, their families, their reputations, their health, and in some cases their freedom.

These ten women came from remarkably different worlds. Monica prayed in Roman North Africa in the fourth century. Teresa of Ávila reformed the Carmelite order in sixteenth-century Spain. Susanna Wesley prayed with her apron drawn over her head in a crowded eighteenth- century Lincolnshire parsonage. Madame Guyon was imprisoned for seven years in the Bastille for her radical devotion to prayer. Amy Carmichael labored fifty-five consecutive years in South India without a furlough. Corrie ten Boom emerged from Ravensbrück concentration camp to preach forgiveness across six continents. Lottie Moon gave herself away in rural China until she had nothing left to give. Mary Slessor faced down headhunters in Nigeria armed only with love and prayer. Gladys Aylward led a hundred children through snow-covered mountains in wartime China when no one else would. Evelyn Christenson built a global prayer movement on a single foundational question. What united them was not their century or their culture or their temperament but their absolute, unshakable conviction that prayer was not peripheral to the Christian life — it was the center of it.

Paul’s instruction to the Colossians applies as urgently to us as it did to them: “Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful” (Colossians 4:2, NIV). The word translated “devote” in the Greek is proskartereo — to persist, to attach oneself to, to be continuously occupied with. It is not the language of casual religious engagement but of committed, daily occupation. These ten women were occupied with prayer. Prayer was not something they did; it was something they were. And through them, God did things that still echo across the centuries.

These chapters are not merely historical portraits. They are invitations. As you read them, you will find yourself standing repeatedly at the edge of a deeper life — a life in which prayer is not a religious duty to be discharged but a living relationship to be inhabited. That life is available to you. Every soul who seeks God with their whole heart finds Him. That is not a motivational sentiment; it is the promise of God, tested by ten thousand lives, and proved again in these ten extraordinary women.

May their lives stir in you a holy dissatisfaction with surface faith. May they make you restless with thin, hurried, mechanical religion. May they send you to your knees with fresh hunger and renewed expectation — and may you discover there the same inexhaustible God these women found waiting for them.

fields.title: Monica of Hippo — The Mother Whose Tears Moved Heaven
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Monica was born in 331 AD in Tagaste, in Roman North Africa — the region that is today Algeria — into a Christian household whose deep faith she absorbed from childhood. She married a pagan Roman official named Patricius and bore him three children, of whom the most famous was Aurelius Augustinus, who would become Saint Augustine of Hippo and one of the greatest theologians in the history of the church. For seventeen years, Monica interceded without ceasing for the conversion of her brilliant, wayward, morally dissolute son, following him from North Africa to Rome to Milan, pursuing him with prayer long after he had fled her presence.

Her tears were so persistent and her faith so visible that a bishop famously told her: “The child of those tears shall never perish.” He was right. Augustine converted in 386 AD, and Monica died the following year at Ostia, at peace, her life’s great work complete.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Monica did not write theological treatises or deliver sermons. Her teaching on prayer was the teaching of her life — a living demonstration, conducted across two decades, of what it looks like to bring an impossible burden before God and refuse to let it go. The lesson she teaches every generation is the lesson of persevering intercession: that love and faith together can sustain prayer long past the point at which hope seems reasonable, and that the God who delays is not the God who has forgotten.

The scriptural ground of Monica’s intercession was not a single verse but the whole character of God as a Father who receives the cries of His children. Jesus’ parable of the persistent widow was not a metaphor to Monica — it was a calling. Her pattern of prayer embodied the imperative: “that they should always pray and not give up” (Luke 18:1, NIV). Seventeen years is a long time to pray for one person’s soul. Monica prayed through seasons in which Augustine moved not toward God but further from Him — joining the Manichaeans, taking a concubine, pursuing academic glory in Carthage, Rome, and Milan. Each new development was a new test of her faith, and each time she returned to her knees with the same petition, the same tears, and the same undiminished expectation.

Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, who would eventually be the instrument of Augustine’s conversion, recognized in Monica something rare. Her prayer life was not the performance of religious duty but the outpouring of a heart wholly devoted to God and to the son God had given her. The Psalmist’s image was her reality: “You keep track of all my sorrows. You have collected all my tears in your bottle. You have recorded each one in your book” (Psalm 56:8, NLT). Monica believed this not as poetic sentiment but as literal fact. Every tear she wept over Augustine was a prayer God had heard and recorded. None of it was wasted. The account was building toward an answer.

Her persistent intercession reflected a deep theology of God’s compassion toward the lost. Paul’s words in 1 Timothy captured her burden precisely: “I urge, then, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving be made for all people — for kings and all those in authority, that we may live peaceful and quiet lives in all godliness and holiness. This is good, and pleases God our Saviour, who wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:1–4, NIV). Monica grasped that intercessory prayer for the lost was not an optional supplement to the Christian life but a central obligation — one rooted in the heart of a God who genuinely desires every soul to be saved.

Augustine himself wrote of his mother’s prayer life with awe in his Confessions , describing how her weeping before God on his behalf was more fervent than the weeping of most mothers over the physical death of a child. She understood the stakes. A soul bound for hell was a greater emergency than any temporal catastrophe. Lamentations expressed her spirit perfectly: “Arise, cry out in the night, as the watches of the night begin; pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord” (Lamentations 2:19, NIV). Monica poured herself out — completely, unceasingly — and God received every drop.

The vindication of Monica’s long intercession was not merely the conversion of one brilliant man, though that alone would have justified a lifetime of prayer. It was the reversal that her perseverance proved possible: the demonstration that no heart is too hardened, no life too far gone, no sin too entrenched for the God who answers prayer. The Psalmist’s promise was proved in her life: “Those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy. Those who go out weeping, carrying seed to sow, will return with songs of joy, carrying sheaves with them” (Psalm 126:5–6, NIV). Monica sowed in tears for seventeen years.

The harvest she reaped — the conversion of a man whose writings would shape Christian theology for fifteen centuries — was immeasurably beyond anything she could have asked or imagined.

A Prayer: Lord God, You are a Father who never tires of hearing us. Teach us the holy stubbornness of Monica — to bring the same soul, the same burden, the same need before You day after day, year after year, until Your answer arrives. Where we are tempted to give up, renew our faith. Where we weep over the lost, remind us that You keep every tear. And may we live to see the harvests that our prayers are planting. Amen.

fields.title: Teresa of Ávila — The Mystic Who Built a School of Prayer
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Teresa of Ávila was born on March 28, 1515, in Ávila, Castile, Spain, into a wealthy family of Jewish-Christian heritage. She entered the Carmelite Convent of the Incarnation at twenty and spent nearly twenty years in spiritual mediocrity before a profound encounter with God at the age of thirty-nine transformed her prayer life irrevocably. She became one of the most remarkable contemplative mystics in Christian history, reforming the Carmelite order and founding seventeen convents, all while suffering severe physical illness and fierce ecclesiastical opposition. Her major works — The Interior Castle, The Way of Perfection, and her autobiography — remain among the most profound guides to the life of prayer ever written, and in 1970 she became the first woman to be named a Doctor of the Church by the Roman Catholic tradition.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Teresa’s central conviction was that mental prayer — the interior conversation of the soul with God — was not the special preserve of mystics, nuns, and the spiritually advanced. It was the birthright of every Christian who was willing to enter the interior room where God waits. She described mental prayer as nothing other than “a close sharing between friends; it means taking time frequently to be alone with Him who we know loves us.” This definition democratized contemplation: it asked not for ecstasy or visions but for friendship, trust, and the willingness to be present to God.

The scriptural foundation of Teresa’s approach was the invitation of Christ Himself: “But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you” (Matthew 6:6, NIV). The “room” Jesus described was, for Teresa, not merely a physical space but an interior one — the innermost chamber of the soul where God already dwells and where the deepest prayer happens in silence, beyond words. She taught her sisters that the most important discipline in the Christian life was the willingness to enter that room daily and remain there in receptive, loving attention to the One who waits within.

Teresa’s famous image in The Interior Castle — the soul as a crystal castle with seven dwelling places, the innermost of which is the dwelling of God Himself — was her extended meditation on the prayer of union. She taught that God draws the soul progressively inward through increasing degrees of prayer, from vocal prayer through meditation to contemplation, until in the deepest state the soul rests in an awareness of divine presence that words cannot capture. This journey was not automatic or effortless; it required sustained cooperation, the surrender of self- will, and the willingness to endure what she called “arid” seasons when prayer felt dry and God seemed absent. Yet she was insistent: “The important thing is not to think much but to love much; do, then, whatever most arouses you to love.”

She was deeply practical about the discipline required to sustain the prayer life she described.

The soul that drifts in and out of prayer based on feeling will never go deep. She quoted Psalm 46:10 with particular force — “Be still, and know that I am God” — as the posture that made genuine contemplation possible. To be still, she taught, was not passivity but the most active of spiritual disciplines: the deliberate setting aside of distraction, self-concern, and noise in order to attend to the One who is always already speaking. Her sisters at the reformed Carmelite convents were trained in this discipline from their first days, and Teresa herself spent hours each day in this practice regardless of how many convents she was founding, how many letters she was writing, or how great her physical suffering was.

Her theology of suffering in prayer was among her most important contributions. Teresa experienced debilitating illness throughout her life — including what appears to have been a period of near-death at thirty-seven — and she came to understand suffering not as an obstacle to the prayer life but as one of its primary schools. She found profound comfort in Paul’s paradox: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’

Therefore I will boast all the more gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9, NIV). The weaknesses that made her incapable of managing her own affairs were, she discovered, the very conditions in which God most powerfully took over the management of everything. She wrote to her sisters: “God walks among the pots and pans.”

The ordinary, the painful, and the unglamorous were all raw material for the praying life.

Perhaps most lastingly, Teresa taught that prayer was not preparation for action but was itself the highest and most fruitful form of action available to the human soul. Jesus’ words to His disciples — “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5, NIV) — were for Teresa not a rebuke but a release: a declaration that the soul which remained in God did not need to drive itself frantically toward results. The results were God’s business. The soul’s business was to abide — to remain in the vine — and trust that fruit would come in its season. Her reformed convents, which seemed to the outside world like quiet retreats from the urgent business of the church, were, she insisted, the engine rooms of everything.

A Prayer: Lord Jesus, You have made Your home within us and You invite us to make our home in You. Teach us to be still. Teach us to resist the tyranny of noise and busyness and to enter the interior room where You wait with patience and love. In our weakness, be our strength. In our aridity, be our living water. Draw us ever deeper into the castle of Your love. Amen.

fields.title: Susanna Wesley — The Mother of Methodism
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Susanna Annesley Wesley was born on January 20, 1669, in London, the twenty-fifth child of a prominent Nonconformist minister whose theological library and disciplined household shaped her intellectual and spiritual formation from infancy. She married Samuel Wesley in 1688, and the two moved to Epworth, Lincolnshire, where she bore nineteen children, nine of whom survived to adulthood. Two of her sons — John and Charles Wesley — would become the founders of the Methodist movement and among the most influential Christians of the eighteenth century, but Susanna was their first and most formative teacher. She took seriously the ancient principle: “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it” (Proverbs 22:6, NIV). This was not merely a parenting strategy for her but a theology of intercession: the belief that a parent’s prayers, consistently and earnestly offered over a child from their earliest years, shape the contours of that child’s spiritual life in ways that no subsequent influence can entirely undo. She prayed for her children by name, with specific petitions, and expected God to answer.

Her discipline was extraordinary by any measure. Two hours of daily prayer in the context of a household with up to ten surviving children, limited income, and a frequently absent husband was not the fruit of convenient circumstances but of iron conviction. She seems to have taken the psalmist’s declaration as a personal commitment: “I rise before dawn and cry for help; I have put my hope in your word” (Psalm 119:147, NIV). Prayer for Susanna was not squeezed into the gaps of a busy life but was the foundation around which everything else was organized. She wrote in a letter: “However few were my talents, I could make no return for God’s great love but to give those talents back — and the greatest of them I have is time.”

This conviction was itself a form of prayer — an act of trust in God’s sovereign purposes: “For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future” (Jeremiah 29:11, NIV). She prayed those plans into reality before she knew what they were.

Susanna also held a robust theology of corporate prayer and its power to shape community. Her legacy, ultimately, was not only the conversion and ministry of her children but the living proof that faithfulness in invisible, unglamorous, daily prayer produces fruit beyond the imagining of the one who plants. From her eighteen feet of domestic prayer space, revival spread to a nation and then to the world.

Where we feel the smallness of our circumstances, enlarge our faith. Where our prayers seem too domestic and too hidden to matter, remind us of Susanna — that the prayers of one devoted mother can shape the course of generations. Give us the discipline to give You our best time, and the faith to believe that nothing offered to You in secret is wasted. Amen.

fields.title: Madame Guyon — The Prisoner Whose Spirit Could Not Be Confined
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Jeanne-Marie Bouvières de la Mothe Guyon was born on April 13, 1648, in Montargis, France, into a wealthy family and married at fifteen to a much older man whose household she managed through twelve years of difficult married life until his death in 1676. From early childhood she had experienced an intense interior life of prayer, and after her husband’s death she devoted herself entirely to God, traveling through France and Savoy teaching a form of contemplative prayer she called “quiet prayer” or “pure love.” Her influence was vast, drawing followers from the French aristocracy and the highest ranks of the Catholic clergy, but her teachings also drew fierce ecclesiastical opposition. She was imprisoned in the Bastille from 1698 to 1703 — four years in solitary confinement — and wrote some of her most luminous works from her cell. She was released in 1703 and spent her final years in peaceful exile at Blois, writing until her death in 1717 at sixty-eight.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Madame Guyon’s central teaching was the prayer of simplicity — a form of interior prayer in which the soul ceases its self-directed activity and rests in God, not by emptying the mind but by turning the whole attention lovingly toward the divine presence already dwelling within. She distinguished this from the prayer of effort, in which the soul labors to produce the right words, feelings, or thoughts. Pure prayer, she taught, was not produced by the soul but received — the natural overflow of a heart that had learned to rest in God rather than striving to reach Him.

The great discovery of Guyon’s prayer life was that the circumstances of outward life — including imprisonment, loss, and suffering — had no power over the interior life of a soul truly surrendered to God. She found in Paul’s words her own testimony: “I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content. I know how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Philippians 4:11–12, KJV adapted). The Bastille could imprison her body but could not reach her spirit. She wrote in her autobiography that the years of her imprisonment were among the most joyful of her life, because in the enforced silence and solitude she had found a depth of communion with God that the busy freedom of her earlier years had never produced. “The soul that is truly submitted to God,” she wrote, “finds a paradise in every prison.”

Her book Experiencing the Depths of Jesus Christ — written in just a few days by her own account, as if dictated by the Spirit — taught readers to approach Scripture and prayer not with analytical scrutiny but with receptive, loving attention. She compared this approach to eating: the goal of reading Scripture in prayer was not to accumulate information but to be nourished. Jesus’ words to His disciples expressed her deepest conviction about the basis of this prayer life: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know his master’s business. Instead, I have called you friends, for everything that I learned from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15, NIV). The praying soul was not a supplicant working to gain access to a reluctant sovereign but a friend received into the most intimate confidence of God. This friendship was the soil in which all genuine prayer grew.

Guyon’s teaching on suffering as the refinery of prayer had a depth born from personal experience. She lost her beauty to smallpox, her freedom to imprisonment, her reputation to controversy, and her influence to ecclesiastical condemnation — and through each loss she found not a diminished prayer life but a purified one. She clung to the great promise of Isaiah: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you pass through the rivers, they will not sweep over you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned; the flames will not set you ablaze” (Isaiah 43:2, NIV). These were not, for Guyon, words of comfort to be received gratefully from a distance. They were a precise description of her own biography, tested and proved in the waters and fires of her actual life.

She was insistent that the deepest prayer required the most complete surrender of self. The soul that approached God still clutching its own agenda, its own plans, its own comfort — even its own spiritual ambitions — would find its access to the depths of God blocked by the very things it was carrying. She found in Paul’s extraordinary words in Philippians the peace that resulted from this surrender: “And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7, NIV). That transcendent peace was not the peace of good circumstances but the peace of a will fully yielded — a soul that had stopped arguing with God about the terms of its life and had accepted, with love, whatever He sent.

Her final legacy was the proof she provided — through her own extraordinary life — that no external power can truly confine the soul that has learned to pray from the inside out. The world’s most secure prison could not silence Madame Guyon’s prayer or diminish her joy. She was, in the fullest sense, free — as Paul testified from his own imprisonment: “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17, NIV).

Where the Spirit of the Lord is, every prison becomes a sanctuary.

A Prayer: Lord of all freedom, teach us the prayer that no circumstance can interrupt. When outward conditions are hard, draw us into the inner room where You are always present and always near. Deliver us from the slavery of needing comfortable circumstances in order to pray, and show us instead the joy of the soul that has found its home in You alone. Amen.

fields.title: Amy Carmichael — The Missionary Who Prayed Without Ceasing
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born on December 16, 1867, in Millisle, County Down, Ireland, the eldest of seven children in a deeply devout Presbyterian family. After a profound spiritual experience in her youth, she gave herself to mission work, serving briefly in Japan and Ceylon before arriving in South India in 1895 — where she remained for the next fifty-five years without a single furlough. She founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in Tamil Nadu, initially to rescue young girls from temple prostitution, which grew into a community of over nine hundred people providing a home for children who had nowhere else to go. She spent the last twenty years of her life largely bedridden following a serious fall in 1931, writing over thirty books of verse and devotion from her room that became beloved spiritual classics across the world. She died in 1951 at the age of eighty-three, having never left India after first arriving.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Amy Carmichael’s prayer life was the hidden architecture of everything visible at Dohnavur. She described prayer as the primary work of the fellowship, more fundamental than feeding the children, teaching in the schools, or building the houses. Every significant decision was made on the knees. Every child received into the community was prayed for by name. Every crisis was met first in prayer before it was met in action. She told her coworkers: “Prayer is the core of our day. Take prayer out and the day would collapse, would be pithless as a hollow reed.”

Carmichael’s foundational conviction was that the Christian life, in its essence, is the life of Christ continued through the believer who has surrendered to Him. She drew this directly from Paul’s declaration: “I have been crucified with Christ and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The life I now live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20, NIV). If Christ lived in her, then her prayer was His prayer. Her love for the children at Dohnavur was His love extended through her hands. Her suffering was participation in His sufferings. This integration of identity with Christ was not mystical abstraction for Carmichael but daily, practical, grounding truth — the solid floor beneath everything she did.

Her approach to intercessory prayer was marked by extraordinary specificity and persistence.

She prayed for individual children, for their particular spiritual struggles, for the specific communities they had come from, and for the cultural strongholds that kept those communities in spiritual darkness. She was certain that this kind of targeted, persistent intercession was what Luke described when he recorded Jesus’ instruction: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into his harvest field” (Luke 10:2, NIV). She was not only a worker in the harvest but a persistent asker for more workers, writing letters across the world calling for reinforcements and sustaining those requests in prayer long after the letters had been sent.

Her bedridden years were not, by her own account, a diminishment of her prayer life but its intensification. When she could no longer walk the compound, visit the children, or attend the meetings, she could still pray — and she did, for hours each day. She took profound comfort in the character of the God she addressed: “So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand” (Isaiah 41:10, NIV). The same God who had sustained her through fifty years of active missionary service was fully capable of making her years of enforced stillness equally fruitful.

She believed this and wrote books from her bed that have introduced thousands of readers to the life of prayer she had lived.

Carmichael’s vision of the cost of discipleship was unflinching. She had left Ireland knowing she might never return. She had watched children die in her arms. She had been misrepresented, opposed, and worn down by decades of spiritual warfare. Yet she held to the words of Jesus without flinching: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23, NIV). The cross, she wrote, was not merely a metaphor for inconvenience. It was the willingness to be spent entirely in the service of the One who had been spent entirely for you. Her prayer life was the inner form of that spending — the daily, complete giving of herself to God in communion before giving herself to His work in service.

Her final teaching, distilled from the whole of a life given without reservation, was this: God can be trusted with everything. Whatever He allows — the pain, the loss, the limitation, the long years without visible fruit — is working toward something that love has prepared. She held to Paul’s great confidence: “And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28, NIV). She had tested this promise in conditions severe enough to disprove it, and found it true. That confidence fueled her prayer until her last breath.

A Prayer: Lord Jesus, who gave Yourself without reservation for us, teach us to give ourselves without reservation to You. Where we cling to comfort and convenience, loosen our grip. Where we are tempted to measure our worth by what we accomplish, remind us that the greatest work is done on our knees. Let the life we live be Yours — lived by faith, sustained by prayer, spent in love. Amen.

fields.title: Corrie ten Boom — Prayer in the Shadow of the Death Camp
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Cornelia “Corrie” ten Boom was born on April 15, 1892, in Haarlem, the Netherlands, into a watchmaker’s family known throughout the city for their Christian faith and hospitality. She trained as a watchmaker — becoming the first licensed female watchmaker in the Netherlands — and lived a quiet, devout life until the Nazi occupation of Holland. In 1942, the ten Boom family began hiding Jewish refugees in a secret room behind Corrie’s bedroom, sheltering over eight hundred people over two years before being betrayed and arrested in 1944. Corrie and her beloved sister Betsie were transported to Ravensbrück concentration camp, where Betsie died in December 1944. Corrie was released in a clerical error just days before women her age were sent to the gas chambers, and she spent the next thirty-five years of her life traveling to sixty-four countries, telling what she called the greatest story in the world — that there is no pit so deep that God’s love is not deeper still.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Corrie ten Boom’s teaching on prayer was born, not in a library, but in a flea-infested barracks in the worst death camp the Nazi regime operated. What she discovered in those conditions was a truth she spent the rest of her life reporting: that prayer is not a practice that depends on circumstances, and that the God who meets us in prayer is not diminished or distanced by the darkness of our situation. If anything, she found Him closer in the darkness than in the light.

Her sister Betsie had taught her, in the barracks, to give thanks in everything — even for the fleas, which, they discovered, were the reason the guards avoided their dormitory and allowed the Bible reading and prayer meetings to continue uninterrupted. This was Paul’s instruction taken to its literal extreme: “Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7, NIV). The peace that Paul described as transcending understanding was precisely what Corrie and Betsie experienced in Ravensbrück — a peace that made no rational sense given their circumstances, and was therefore undeniable evidence of God’s active presence.

After her release and the launch of her global speaking ministry, Corrie returned repeatedly to the experience of the camp to ground her teaching on prayer in the most incontrovertible evidence she had: personal survival. She had walked through what the Psalmist called the valley of the shadow of death — not metaphorically but literally — and the Shepherd had been there.

fields.title: Lottie Moon — The Woman Who Gave Everything to China
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Charlotte Diggs “Lottie” Moon was born on December 12, 1840, in Viewmont, Virginia, into a wealthy and prominent Baptist family. She was one of the first women in the American South to earn a master’s degree, and she possessed a formidable intellect and force of personality that could have secured her a comfortable and distinguished academic life. Instead, in 1873, she sailed for China under the Foreign Mission Board of the Southern Baptist Convention and spent the next forty years of her life in Tengchow and then Pingtu, preaching, teaching, and evangelizing in conditions of extreme hardship. When famine struck the region of Shaanxi in 1911–1912, Lottie began giving her own food to starving Chinese neighbors, a practice she continued until she herself was too weak from malnutrition to walk. She died on December 24, 1912, on a ship bringing her home, weighing less than fifty pounds. Today, the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering — raised annually by Southern Baptist churches — has contributed over four billion dollars to international missions.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Lottie Moon’s teaching on prayer was embedded in her passionate theology of mission. She could not separate the two, because she understood prayer as the fuel without which mission would be nothing but human effort, and mission as the arena in which prayer proved its transformative power. She was blunt in her appeals to the churches back home: she did not want only money. She wanted prayer. “Pray for China,” she wrote repeatedly. “Pray for the workers.

Pray that God will call more.” She understood what Jesus meant when He spoke of prayer and mission in the same breath.

The heartbeat of Lottie’s ministry was the conviction that the Great Commission was every Christian’s responsibility, and that intercession for the unreached was not optional but obligatory. She had taken seriously Jesus’ instruction: “The harvest is plentiful but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into his harvest field” (Matthew 9:37–38, NIV). She was asking — constantly, persistently, through her letters and through her prayers — for more workers. And she was also being the answer to her own prayer, investing herself without remainder in the harvest field where God had placed her.

Lottie’s willingness to give her life for the people of China was grounded in a clear-eyed theology of the cross as the model for missionary life. She did not romanticize the sacrifice; she calculated it and accepted it. Jesus’ words were her commission: “Very truly I tell you, unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a single seed. But if it dies, it produces many seeds” (John 12:24, NIV). She was that grain of wheat. She understood that going into the ground was not the end of the story but its beginning. Her death — physical and decades-long — was the seed from which a harvest of millions of dollars for global mission would eventually spring.

In the hardest years of her ministry, when the Chinese were suspicious and hostile, when doors were closed and the work seemed fruitless, Lottie sustained herself in prayer with the certainty that God had not sent her on a fool’s errand. She held to Paul’s confidence: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16, NIV). The power was not hers. She was only the carrier. Her prayer was the means by which she remained connected to the source of the power that she was delivering — and she was meticulous about maintaining that connection.

Lottie also prayed with deep specificity for the people she was trying to reach. She learned the language, immersed herself in the culture, ate the food, wore the clothing, and walked the roads of rural Shandong Province so that her prayers for individuals were prayers formed in love and intimate knowledge. She drew on Paul’s description of mission’s logic: “How, then, can they call on the one they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the one of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone preaching to them? And how can anyone preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14–15, NIV). She was the sent one. Her prayer was the invisible dimension of her proclamation — the act by which the human messenger stayed connected to the divine source.

Her ultimate act of prayer was her death: the laying down of her body in an act of love for those who would never know her name or understand what she had given for them. Paul’s description of the motive driving this kind of self-sacrifice was the best caption for Lottie’s life: “For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that one died for all, and therefore all died” (2 Corinthians 5:14, NIV). She was compelled. Not by guilt, not by duty, but by love. The love of Christ for her, and through her for the people of China.

A Prayer: Lord of the harvest, give us Lottie’s love — the kind that counts the cost and pays it anyway. Where we are comfortable and insulated from the world’s need, disturb us. Where we hold back from sacrifice, show us the cross. Increase our intercession for the unreached, and grant that we, in our own measure, might give as she gave — everything, without regret, for love of You and love of those You came to save. Amen.

fields.title: Mary Slessor — The White Queen Who Prayed Down Strongholds
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Mary Mitchell Slessor was born on December 2, 1848, in Aberdeen, Scotland, the second of seven children of a shoemaker father whose alcoholism cast a long shadow over her childhood.

She worked in a Dundee textile mill from the age of eleven to help support her family, educating herself in the early mornings before her shifts began. After the death of David Livingstone in 1873 stirred her to give her life to Africa, she applied to the Calabar Mission (in present-day Nigeria) and arrived in 1876. Over the next thirty-eight years she moved progressively deeper into unevangelized territory, eventually settling among the Okoyong and Ibibio peoples where no European had previously lived. She learned the languages, adopted the customs, rescued hundreds of twins — killed at birth in local superstition as evil omens — and became so trusted that she was appointed a magistrate by the British government. She died on January 13, 1915, in Use Ikot Oku, Nigeria, where she had lived for years in a simple mud hut, and was known throughout the region as Ma — Mother.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Mary Slessor prayed with a bluntness and urgency that matched her personality. She prayed on her knees, she prayed aloud in the night, she prayed over sleeping children, and she prayed standing between armed warriors who were about to kill each other. Her prayer life was not separated from her daily existence but woven through every moment of it — an ongoing conversation with a God she treated not with formal distance but with the intimacy of a child addressing a trusted, powerful, and entirely available Father.

Slessor’s willingness to go where no one else would go, to face dangers that most missionaries refused to approach, was rooted in a specific confidence about the character of God. She had received God’s call in the same terms God had always issued it: “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the Lord your God will be with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9, NIV). She took this promise with absolute literalism. The remote villages of Calabar were not beyond the reach of this promise. The midnight confrontations with armed men were not outside the jurisdiction of the God who had spoken these words. She went because she believed God went with her, and the evidence she accumulated over thirty-eight years confirmed that belief beyond any reasonable doubt.

Her intercessory prayers had a quality of holy boldness that came from deep familiarity with the God to whom she spoke. She did not pray politely. She prayed urgently, with the directness of someone who knew that lives depended on the answer. She had absorbed Isaiah’s account of God’s open invitation: “Here am I. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8, NIV) — and she had said it, and God had sent her, and now she prayed with the authority of someone who was fully, consciously operating under divine commission. Her prayers over specific people, specific situations, and specific spiritual strongholds in Calabar were not hesitant suggestions but earnest, authoritative intercessions made in the name of the One who had sent her.

One of the most documented aspects of her ministry was her practice of inserting herself physically between warring parties and praying while the crisis unfolded around her. She trusted completely that God’s Spirit could accomplish in seconds what human diplomacy might require months to achieve. She operated from the conviction that Zechariah expressed: “Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit” says the Lord Almighty (Zechariah 4:6, NIV). No human strength, no political authority, no physical barrier was ultimately decisive in the face of the Spirit’s presence. Her prayers were the means by which that presence was invited and released into situations that would have overwhelmed any merely human intervention.

Mary Slessor also prayed with extraordinary persistence for the communities she served. She had lived among the Okoyong for years before she saw the first converts — years in which nothing visibly changed, in which the old practices and the old fears seemed impenetrable. She held to the promise that no darkness was ultimate: “The people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death a light has dawned” (Matthew 4:16, NIV). She prayed the light down. She stayed long past the point at which most missionaries would have concluded that the field was unfruitful. And eventually — always eventually — the light broke through.

Her legacy is the legacy of every missionary intercessor who has gone where it was not safe, stayed where it was not comfortable, and prayed where it was not easy. She embodied in her person the principle that Hebrews celebrates in its great cloud of witnesses: “who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, quenched the fury of the flames, and escaped the edge of the sword; whose weakness was turned to strength; and who became powerful in battle” (Hebrews 11:33–34, NIV). Mary Slessor’s weakness — a small, red-haired Scottish mill worker — was turned to extraordinary strength, and strongholds that had stood for generations fell before her prayers.

A Prayer: Lord God, give us the courage of Mary Slessor — to go where we are sent, to stay when we are tested, and to pray when all human resources are exhausted. Where we are intimidated by the darkness around us, remind us that You have conquered it. Where we are tempted to retreat from the difficult field, give us the holy stubbornness that refuses to abandon what You have commissioned. May our weakness become Your strength. Amen.

fields.title: Gladys Aylward — The Unlikely Missionary Who Walked by Faith
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Gladys May Aylward was born on February 24, 1902, in Edmonton, Middlesex, England, the daughter of a postman. She worked as a parlour maid and felt a persistent call to missionary work in China, but when she applied to the China Inland Mission in 1929 she was rejected on the grounds that she was too old to learn the language and lacked the necessary academic qualifications. Undeterred, she saved her wages and in 1930 traveled alone by the cheapest route available — overland through Siberia by train during the Sino-Soviet conflict — to Yangcheng, Shanxi Province, where an elderly missionary named Jeannie Lawson welcomed her. Over the following years she became an innkeeper, an official government foot inspector for the Chinese authorities, and — most famously — the woman who in 1940 led approximately one hundred orphaned children over the mountains to safety during the Japanese invasion, a journey of twelve days on foot over the Shanxi mountains. She spent the rest of her life caring for Chinese children, eventually from Taiwan, until her death in 1970.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Gladys Aylward’s prayer life was uncomplicated and total. She prayed with the simplicity of a child and the tenacity of a soldier. She had no formal theological training and no learned vocabulary of intercession. What she had was an absolute, unqualified certainty that God heard her, that He was personally interested in her affairs, and that He would do what He promised.

This certainty was not naive; it was the hard-won product of watching God provide for her, protect her, and direct her through circumstances that should, by any rational calculation, have destroyed her.

From the moment she boarded the train to Siberia against all advice and with almost no money, Gladys was operating on a single verse that she returned to throughout her life: “For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future” (Jeremiah 29:11, NIV). The China Inland Mission had decided she had no future in China. God had decided otherwise. She prayed with the confidence of someone whose life was inside a plan too large and too purposeful to be derailed by any institution’s rejection or any obstacle’s resistance.

The mountain crossing with the children in 1940 remains one of the most extraordinary acts of faith-in-prayer in twentieth-century mission history. When they arrived at the Yellow River without a boat and without a military escort, Gladys prayed and waited. A Chinese Nationalist officer eventually arrived with his soldiers and transported them across. She had simply prayed and trusted. Her prayer was grounded in the Psalmist’s confidence: “I lift up my eyes to the mountains — where does my help come from? My help comes from the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:1–2, NIV). Her help did come from the Lord. It came in the form of a Chinese officer and his soldiers, but its origin was the God she had been petitioning since long before they reached the river.

Gladys prayed with an expectation of miracle that could have seemed presumptuous in someone with less evidence. But she had evidence. She had seen God provide food, heal the sick, pacify rioting prisoners, and protect her through artillery bombardment. Her prayer was the prayer of someone who had repeatedly proved the promise of Jesus: “Everything is possible for one who believes” (Mark 9:23, NIV). She believed. And she had watched the impossible become possible often enough that her belief was no longer theoretical. She had a track record with the God of the impossible, and she drew on that track record in prayer with the straightforward confidence of a woman who had learned from experience that God could be trusted.

One of the recurring themes of her prayer life was the willingness to be directed by God into circumstances that made no sense from a human perspective. She had not planned to become a foot inspector, or an innkeeper, or the guardian of a hundred orphaned children. But each step had been God’s leading, and she had followed it in prayer. She took to heart the instruction of Proverbs: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5–6, NIV). Her path had been anything but straightforward by human logic, yet from God’s perspective it was perfectly straight — directed toward the purposes He had ordained before she was born.

Gladys Aylward’s story is one of the great demonstrations that God does not call the equipped; He equips the called. The parlour maid whom the mission board rejected became one of the most celebrated Christian missionaries of the twentieth century — not because of her qualifications but because of her prayers. fields.title: Evelyn Christenson — What Happens When Women Pray
fields.body_html:
Who She Was Evelyn Maxine Wheeler Christenson was born on November 1, 1922, in Muskegon, Michigan, and spent her adult life as a pastor’s wife, raising three children and serving in local church ministry. In 1968, she led a small six-week prayer seminar for women in her home church in St.

Paul, Minnesota, which produced results so dramatic that she was invited to repeat it across the country, then internationally. Her book “What Happens When Women Pray,” published in 1975, became one of the most widely read books on prayer in the twentieth century, eventually selling over two million copies. She founded United Prayer Ministries and spent the next four decades teaching prayer in churches, conferences, and communities across the world, training an estimated fifteen million women in the principles of corporate and personal prayer before her death in 2013. She was not a seminary-trained theologian or a famous preacher; she was a pastor’s wife who asked a simple question and devoted her life to the answer.

Her Core Teaching on Prayer Evelyn Christenson’s teaching on prayer was built around the simplest possible question: what actually happens when we pray? Not what should happen theologically, not what has happened historically in famous revivals, but what happens right now, in ordinary churches, when ordinary Christians pray together with genuine faith. Her answer, drawn from decades of direct observation, was consistent and compelling: extraordinary things happen. Walls come down.

Relationships are healed. Addictions are broken. Churches are transformed. Communities are changed. Prayer works — and the evidence for this is available to anyone willing to pray long enough to observe the results.

Her foundational scripture was the great promise of James, which she quoted in virtually every seminar, every book, and every teaching opportunity: “The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective” (James 5:16, NIV). She built her entire ministry on the conviction that this was not aspirational language but a factual description of reality. Prayer was not merely spiritually meaningful; it was causally powerful. Things happened as a direct result of prayer that would not have happened without it. This conviction was not mystical but practical, grounded in Scripture and confirmed by the thousands of testimonies she collected from women who had prayed and seen God answer.

One of Christenson’s most important contributions was her recovery of the New Testament pattern of corporate prayer. She observed that the early church — from the upper room prayer meeting before Pentecost through the whole of Acts — prayed together as a community, not merely as isolated individuals. She pointed her students to the extraordinary promise attached to this practice: “Again, truly I tell you that if two of you on earth agree about anything they ask for, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. For where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them” (Matthew 18:19–20, NIV). The gathering of two or three in prayer was not a consolation for the absence of large congregations — it was a specific and powerful configuration that Christ had personally endorsed with His presence. Christenson spent her ministry mobilizing those twos and threes.

Her teaching on listening in prayer — the often-neglected second half of the conversation — was particularly valuable. Most people, she observed, come to prayer with a list of requests and leave when the list is exhausted, without waiting to hear what God might want to say. She urged her students to practice the discipline of silence in prayer, of “two-way prayer” in which the believer speaks and then waits. She grounded this in the instruction of 1 John: “This is the confidence we have in approaching God: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us — whatever we ask — we know that we have what we asked of him” (1 John 5:14–15, NIV). Praying according to His will required first knowing His will — and knowing His will required listening.

Christenson also taught persistently on the relationship between prayer and personal holiness.

She had observed that the prayer lives of most Christians were hampered not by lack of technique or information but by unconfessed sin and unresolved relational fractures that blocked the free flow of communication with God. She drew on Paul’s instruction to the church at Colossae: “Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful” (Colossians 4:2, NIV).

The “watchfulness” Paul described included watchfulness over the interior life — the attitudes, the grudges, the pride, and the self-deceptions that, left unaddressed, silently undermined the prayer life from within.

Her lasting legacy is the hundreds of thousands of prayer groups that formed as a result of her teaching, sustained long after the original seminar by communities of women who had discovered for themselves that her simple thesis was true. She had not promised them mystical experiences or dramatic miracles; she had simply invited them to pray and to observe what God would do. They prayed. They observed. They kept praying. The early church’s pattern was hers: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42, NIV). Devotion to prayer, practiced together, transforms everything it touches.

A Prayer: Lord, make us women and men who ask — and keep asking. Teach us to gather with even two or three in Your name and trust that You are present and working.

Show us not only how to speak our requests but how to listen for Your answers.

Where our prayer lives are thin and infrequent, deepen them. Where we are isolated, give us the body of Christ to pray alongside us. And let us discover, as Evelyn did, what happens when Your people truly pray. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion: The Invitation Still Stands
fields.body_html:
You have now met ten women whose lives were remarkable in ways that history has largely confirmed. Monica’s tears produced a theologian whose influence has never ceased. Teresa’s interior castle still guides seekers centuries after her death. Susanna’s domestic prayer cell ignited a revival that spread across the English-speaking world. Madame Guyon’s writings from a Bastille prison cell have introduced millions of readers to the depths of contemplative prayer.

Amy Carmichael’s fifty-five years of unbroken service in India continue to inspire and convict those who read her story. Corrie ten Boom’s Ravensbrück testimony has encouraged the faith of countless people walking through their own valleys of shadow. Lottie Moon’s sacrificial death seeded a missions offering that has funded thousands of workers across the world. Mary Slessor’s courage among the headhunters of Calabar broke open an entire region to the gospel.

Gladys Aylward’s mountain crossing with a hundred children remains one of the great acts of faith in recorded history. Evelyn Christenson’s simple question has mobilized an estimated fifteen million people to pray.

What do you do with lives like these? You cannot simply admire them from a distance, because each of them would refuse the admiration. Each of them, in her own way, would deflect every tribute back to the God who had answered her prayers, given her the faith to pray them, and produced the results that others were now praising. They were, to a woman, deeply convinced that what they had discovered was available to everyone — that the God who had met them in their specific centuries, cultures, and circumstances was the same God available to every human being willing to seek Him.

That is the most important thing this book is trying to say. These ten women were not exceptional because they possessed some spiritual gift that most people lack. They were exceptional because they took God at His word when He said: “You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13, NIV). They sought Him with their whole hearts. And they found Him. The promise has not been withdrawn. It stands today exactly as it stood when Monica wept in Carthage, when Teresa prayed in Ávila, when Susanna drew her apron over her head in Epworth, when Gladys prayed at the Yellow River. The invitation still stands.

Perhaps you have read this book because prayer has been a struggle for you. Perhaps it has felt dry, mechanical, or simply absent from your life — a discipline you know you should practice but find yourself repeatedly failing to sustain. If so, these ten women have a message for you: begin again. Begin now. The God who met Corrie ten Boom in a concentration camp is not waiting for you to achieve a certain level of spiritual attainment before He will meet you. He meets you where you are. He receives the broken, halting, five-minute prayer of a beginner with the same attentive love with which He received the long intercessory vigils of John Hyde.

Perhaps you have read this book because you are already a person of prayer, seeking encouragement and example to go deeper. If so, the ten women in these pages are calling you further in. There is always more. Teresa of Ávila described rooms within rooms within rooms in the interior castle of the soul, and she had walked them all — and beyond the last room she had found not a wall but an opening into the infinite. No one exhausts God. No one reaches the end of what prayer can discover or accomplish. There is always deeper water to swim in.

For every reader, whatever your starting point, the invitation is the same. It is not complicated. It does not require a theological degree, a spiritual director, or a particular temperament. It requires only what these ten women brought to it: sincerity, persistence, and the willingness to take God at His word. Jesus said it as simply as it can be said: “Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened” (Matthew 7:7–8, NIV).

Everyone. Not the spiritually gifted. Not the monastically inclined. Not the theologically trained.

Everyone who asks receives. Everyone who seeks finds. Everyone who knocks will find the door opened. Monica asked. Teresa sought. Susanna knocked. The door opened for each of them. It will open for you.

“You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart.”

— Jeremiah 29:13 (NIV)
